entries.finding: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis included 11 randomized controlled trials with 870 participants with knee osteoarthritis, with 451 assigned to collagen supplementation and 419 to placebo.
Collagen supplementation improved pooled knee-osteoarthritis function scores versus placebo (MD -6.46; 95% CI -9.52 to -3.40; p=0.00001), with substantial heterogeneity (I²=75%).
Collagen supplementation improved pooled pain scores versus placebo (MD -13.63; 95% CI -20.67 to -6.58; p=0.00001), with high heterogeneity (I²=88%).

The high I² values for both function and pain indicate substantial between-trial variability, so the pooled benefits should not be treated as uniform across collagen preparations, study populations, or trial designs.

The review searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Scopus through October 2023 and used the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool; its conclusion was limited to symptomatic knee-osteoarthritis outcomes from oral collagen-based supplements.
A 2025 GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated randomized controlled trials of spirulina supplementation in adults for systolic and diastolic blood pressure outcomes.
Spirulina supplementation reduced systolic blood pressure by a pooled WMD of -4.41 mmHg (95% CI -6.74 to -2.07), with moderate heterogeneity (I²=66.1%).
Spirulina supplementation reduced diastolic blood pressure by a pooled WMD of -2.84 mmHg (95% CI -4.65 to -1.03), with moderate heterogeneity (I²=62.3%).

Subgroup analyses continued to favor lower systolic and diastolic pressure in participants with elevated baseline blood pressure, hypertension, overweight, age over 50 years, and interventions lasting more than eight weeks.

GRADE rated the blood-pressure evidence as moderate quality; dose-response and meta-regression analyses were not significant because of limited study and participant numbers, and the authors called for additional high-quality randomized trials.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included 15 studies of alpha-lipoic acid for diabetic polyneuropathy, with 12 studies contributing outcome data; 19 of 23 analyzed outcomes significantly favored alpha-lipoic acid at one or more doses.
Alpha-lipoic acid improved Total Symptom Score paresthesia versus comparator with an SMD of -1.04 (95% CI -1.24 to -0.84; p<0.00001).
Alpha-lipoic acid produced a smaller but statistically significant improvement in Total Symptom Score numbness (SMD -0.23; 95% CI -0.44 to -0.01; p=0.04).
Alpha-lipoic acid improved the Hamburg Pain Adjective List outcome with an SMD of -1.00 (95% CI -1.15 to -0.85; p<0.00001).

HbA1c, nitric oxide, sural sensory nerve action potential, and peroneal motor nerve conduction velocity did not significantly change; symptom improvements were especially evident around 600 mg/day, while effects on nerve conduction and long-term glycemic control remained inconclusive.

A 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis included 20 randomized controlled trials with 1,633 participants evaluating Curcuma longa, Boswellia serrata, or mixed formulations for knee osteoarthritis.
Modified Curcuma longa formulations reduced visual-analog-scale pain versus placebo with an SMD of -2.82 (95% CI -5.30 to -0.33).
Modified Boswellia serrata formulations significantly improved WOMAC pain, stiffness, and knee-function outcomes compared with other intervention groups in the network meta-analysis.
No statistically significant differences in adverse events were observed among the Curcuma, Boswellia, mixed-formulation, placebo, or comparator groups evaluated in the network.

The authors concluded that Boswellia extract, especially modified formulations, improved joint function and that only modified Curcuma formulations showed notable pain reduction; benefits of combined Curcuma-Boswellia preparations remained insufficiently established.

A 2025 GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis included 11 randomized controlled trials evaluating resveratrol effects on human SIRT1 gene expression, protein expression, or serum levels.
Resveratrol did not significantly change SIRT1 gene expression overall (SMD 0.05; 95% CI -0.24 to 0.344; p=0.73).
Resveratrol did not significantly change SIRT1 protein expression overall (SMD 0.30; 95% CI -0.15 to 0.77; p=0.18).
Resveratrol did not significantly change serum SIRT1 levels overall (MD -0.04; 95% CI -0.235 to 0.16; p=0.70).

Subgroup analyses suggested higher SIRT1 gene expression in trials shorter than 12 weeks and in blood-tissue measurements, and dose-response analyses suggested regimen dependence; these subgroup signals did not alter the null overall meta-analysis.
